name: Paul the Apostle
desc: Paul, born Saul of Tarsus, was a Christian apostle who spread the teachings of Jesus in the first century CE and founded several Christian communities in Asia Minor and Europe from the mid-40s to the mid-50s. His life is known chiefly from his letters and the Acts of the Apostles. According to Acts, he was a Pharisee who persecuted the followers of Jesus until a vision of Christ on the road to Damascus led him to be baptized. Fourteen New Testament books are traditionally attributed to him, of which scholars regard seven as undisputed. His death in Rome under Nero is traditional, dated either after the fire of 64 or a few years later.

name: Saint Peter
desc: Peter, born Simon bar Jonah, was one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus and one of the first leaders of the early Christian Church. A fisherman and the brother of Andrew, he appears prominently in all four gospels and in Acts, and Jesus gave him the Aramaic name Cephas, meaning rock. Catholic and Orthodox tradition treats him as the first bishop of Rome and of Antioch, and Catholic teaching holds that Jesus promised him a special position. Church Fathers attest that he spent his last years in Rome and, according to tradition, was crucified upside down under Nero. Modern scholarship generally rejects his authorship of the two New Testament letters attributed to him.

name: Pontius Pilate
desc: Pontius Pilate was the fifth Roman governor of Judaea, serving under Emperor Tiberius from 26/27 to 36/37 CE. The gospels, Josephus and Tacitus attribute the crucifixion of Jesus to his orders, and the gospels portray him as reluctant to carry it out. Josephus and Philo record several conflicts with the Jewish population, and Josephus reports that he was dismissed after violently putting down a Samaritan uprising at Mount Gerizim. Little survives of his rule beyond his coins and the Pilate Stone inscription, and his fate after leaving office is unknown. Historians are divided on whether he governed brutally and ineptly or with moderate competence.

name: Mary Magdalene
desc: Mary Magdalene was, according to the four canonical gospels, a woman who travelled with Jesus as one of his followers and witnessed his crucifixion and resurrection. Luke says that seven demons had gone out of her and that she helped support the group from her resources. Her name is usually taken to mean that she came from Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee. In the gospel of John she is the first to see the risen Jesus and is sent to tell the apostles, so some traditions call her the apostle to the apostles. A Western tradition, shaped by a sermon of Pope Gregory I in 591, made her a repentant prostitute, which has no basis in the gospels.

name: Saint Joseph
desc: Joseph, according to the canonical gospels, was a Jewish man of Nazareth in the first century who was married to Mary and was the legal father of Jesus. Matthew and Luke give him differing genealogies and infancy narratives: in Matthew an angel directs him in dreams, including the flight into Egypt, while in Luke he travels to Bethlehem for a census. He last appears when Jesus is twelve, at the Passover visit to the Temple. The gospels call him a tekton, traditionally translated as carpenter, a word that can cover other craftsmen. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran traditions, and Catholics honour him as patron of workers.

name: Judas Iscariot
desc: Judas Iscariot was, according to the four canonical gospels, one of the Twelve Apostles of Jesus. The gospels say he betrayed Jesus to the authorities in Gethsemane with a kiss, and Matthew adds that the price was thirty pieces of silver. Luke and John suggest that Satan had entered him. Matthew says he hanged himself, while Acts gives a different account of his death, and Matthias was later chosen to replace him. The Gnostic Gospel of Judas presents his act as done at Jesus's instruction, and Irenaeus denounced that text as heresy. Most secular historians accept that he existed. His name later became a byword for betrayal and was used to justify Christian antisemitism.

name: Caiaphas
desc: Joseph ben Caiaphas was a high priest in the first century. The Gospels of Matthew, Luke and John present him as an organizer of the plot against Jesus and as presiding over the Sanhedrin trial. Josephus, the most reliable source outside the New Testament, says the Roman prefect Valerius Gratus appointed him in 18 CE and that the legate of Syria Lucius Vitellius later deposed him. His tenure of eighteen years suggests a working relationship with the Romans. In John he is the son-in-law of Annas and argues that it is better for one man to die than for the nation to be destroyed. A limestone ossuary found in 1990 may be his, though some scholars dispute the identification.

name: James, brother of Jesus
desc: James, called the Just, was according to the New Testament a brother of Jesus and the first leader of the church in Jerusalem. Paul knew him personally and mentions him in his letter to the Galatians. Accounts of his death differ: Josephus records that he was stoned in 62 CE on the order of the high priest Ananus ben Ananus, while Hegesippus places his death in 69 and says he was thrown from the Temple pinnacle and clubbed. Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that the brothers of Jesus were cousins or stepbrothers, while others consider James a son of Mary and Joseph. Most agree he is not James, son of Zebedee.

name: Apostles in the New Testament
desc: In the New Testament the apostles, above all the Twelve, were the primary disciples of Jesus. The word comes from the Greek apostolos, meaning a messenger or envoy. The Synoptic Gospels describe Jesus commissioning the Twelve, and the gospels and Acts give four lists of them that differ slightly in names. Peter, James and John formed an inner circle. After Judas Iscariot betrayed Jesus and died, the remaining eleven chose Matthias by lot. Paul, though not one of the Twelve, called himself an apostle, and the New Testament also uses the title for others, among them Barnabas. Christian tradition holds that all the Twelve but John were martyred.

name: Last Supper
desc: The Last Supper is the final meal that, in the gospel accounts, Jesus shared with his apostles in Jerusalem before his crucifixion. The earliest mention is in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, and the gospels place it in the week of Passover. During it Jesus predicts his betrayal and Peter's denial. Paul and the Synoptic Gospels relate that Jesus took bread and gave it to those present, which is the scriptural basis of the Eucharist, while John tells instead of the washing of the apostles' feet. The three Synoptic Gospels describe a Passover meal, which John seems to disagree with, and scholars propose various ways to reconcile them.

name: Sermon on the Mount
desc: The Sermon on the Mount is a discourse of Jesus of Nazareth found in chapters 5 to 7 of the Gospel of Matthew, summarizing his moral teachings. It is the first of five discourses in that gospel and contains the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer in its commonly recited form and the Golden Rule. In Matthew, Jesus goes up a mountain with his disciples, sits down and teaches. Christians have traditionally commemorated the Mount of Beatitudes as the site, though Mount Arbel and the Horns of Hattin have also been suggested. Some Christian traditions see the sermon as the counterpart of the giving of the Ten Commandments on Sinai, and Luke places parts of the material in a different setting.

name: Crucifixion of Jesus
desc: The crucifixion of Jesus was his execution by the Romans in 1st-century Judaea, most likely in 30 CE or 33 CE. The four canonical Gospels say he was arrested, tried before the Sanhedrin, then brought before Pontius Pilate, who sentenced him to be scourged and crucified at Calvary (Golgotha) between two convicted men. Paul is the earliest surviving source, and scholars hold the fact of the crucifixion to be near universally accepted, though not its details. Christians call his suffering and death the Passion and treat it as central to their doctrines of salvation and atonement.

name: Resurrection of Jesus
desc: The resurrection of Jesus is the Christian belief that God raised Jesus from the dead on the third day after his crucifixion. The New Testament does not describe the moment itself, only an empty tomb and appearances to his followers; Paul reports an early creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 that scholars think predates his letter. For Christians it is the central mystery of their faith and is observed at Easter. Some historians assess the visionary experiences of his followers as the impetus for the belief, while many leave the question to faith. Islam generally teaches that Jesus was not crucified but ascended directly to God.

name: Baptism of Jesus
desc: The baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist is described in the three Synoptic Gospels, Matthew, Mark and Luke, and is placed at Al-Maghtas (Bethany Beyond the Jordan), in present-day Jordan. In each, the Spirit descends on Jesus and a voice from Heaven speaks, after which the Gospels place his forty days in the Judean desert. Modern biblical scholars regard the baptism as a historical event assigned a high degree of certainty, and often start from it in studying the historical Jesus. Eastern Christianity commemorates it on 6 January, the feast of Epiphany or Theophany, and Western churches recall it in the following week.

name: Lord's Prayer
desc: The Lord's Prayer, also called the Our Father or Pater Noster, is a central Christian prayer attributed to Jesus. It survives in two versions, in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, and the first-century Didache gives a form close to Matthew's. Most scholars regard it as deriving from the historical Jesus, though they debate how the two versions relate. Matthew's has seven petitions, the first three addressed to God and the other four to human needs, and it is the form used in most Christian worship. Some manuscripts and Protestant usage add a closing doxology, and Orthodox churches use their own.

name: Calvary
desc: Calvary, or Golgotha, was a site outside the walls of Roman Jerusalem where, according to the four canonical Gospels, Jesus was crucified. The names mean "place of the Skull", from the Latin Calvariae and the Aramaic Golgolta. Tradition places it within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, a site traditionally believed to have been identified by the empress Helena, mother of Constantine, on her visit to the Holy Land in 325. In the 19th century Protestant scholars proposed another location near the Garden Tomb, about 500 m to the north. It has been a pilgrimage destination since at least the early medieval period.

name: Gethsemane
desc: Gethsemane is a garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives in East Jerusalem where, according to the four Gospels, Jesus underwent the Agony in the Garden and was arrested before his crucifixion. The name comes from Aramaic or Hebrew words meaning "oil press". Four sites near the western foot of the Mount of Olives are claimed by different denominations, among them the garden of the Catholic Church of All Nations and the Russian Orthodox orchard; modern scholarship acknowledges that the exact location is unknown. It became a focus for early Christian pilgrims, and the Pilgrim of Bordeaux visited it in 333.

name: Capernaum
desc: Capernaum was a fishing village on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, established under the Hasmoneans in the 2nd century BCE, with a population of about 1,500 in the 1st century CE. All four Gospels name it, and the Synoptic Gospels present it as the centre of Jesus' public ministry in Galilee, where he taught in the synagogue and healed. Excavations have found two synagogues built in succession on the same spot and a house turned into a church over the 4th and 5th centuries, which Christian tradition holds was the home of Saint Peter. The village was inhabited until the 11th century and abandoned before the First Crusade.

name: Council of Jerusalem
desc: The Council of Jerusalem, or Apostolic Council, is a meeting described in chapter 15 of the Acts of the Apostles and held in Jerusalem about 48–50 CE. According to Acts, it addressed whether Gentile converts had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses, a question raised by the mission of Paul and Barnabas. It decided that they did not, but told them to abstain from food associated with idols, from blood and strangled meat, and from porneia; these instructions are known as the Apostolic Decree. Scholars increasingly affirm the council as historical, but disagree on whether Galatians 2 describes the same event.

name: Conversion of Paul the Apostle
desc: The conversion of Paul the Apostle was, according to the New Testament, the event that led Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had intensely persecuted the followers of Jesus, to become one himself. Acts describes him travelling to Damascus with a mandate from the High Priest when a light from heaven flashed around him; Paul's own letters, including Galatians and 1 Corinthians, speak of a revelation from Jesus Christ and of seeing the risen Christ. Both sources say he had not known Jesus before the crucifixion, and Acts suggests the conversion came four to seven years after it. The accounts describe it as miraculous or revelatory in nature.

name: Pauline epistles
desc: The Pauline epistles are the thirteen books of the New Testament attributed to Paul the Apostle, among the earliest extant Christian documents. Most scholars believe Paul wrote seven of them: Galatians, Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philemon, Philippians and 1 Thessalonians, with consensus dates from about 48 CE for Galatians. Scholars are about evenly divided on 2 Thessalonians, Colossians and Ephesians, and many regard 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus as written in his name by others. The Epistle to the Hebrews was traditionally counted as Paul's, but few scholars now ascribe it to him. They are foundational texts for Christian theology and ethics.

name: Annunciation
desc: The Annunciation is the event in which, according to the Gospel of Luke, the angel Gabriel told Mary that she would conceive and bear a son, Jesus, through a virgin birth. Luke places it in Nazareth in the sixth month of Elizabeth's pregnancy with John the Baptist; Matthew gives a separate, briefer announcement by an angel to Joseph. Many Christians observe the Feast of the Annunciation on 25 March, nine months before Christmas. Gabriel's greeting forms the first part of the Hail Mary prayer. The Annunciation was a major subject in Christian art, especially in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.

name: Assumption of Mary
aka: Dormition of the Mother of God
desc: The Assumption of Mary is the Catholic dogma that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was taken body and soul into heaven. Pope Pius XII defined it on 1 November 1950 in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus, leaving open whether she died first. Eastern Christianity holds the equivalent belief as the Dormition, or Falling Asleep, of the Mother of God, and the feast is kept on 15 August. The New Testament is silent on the end of her life; accounts appear in apocryphal Dormition narratives that scholars date from the fourth century or earlier, and the Emperor Maurice established the feast in Constantinople in 600.

name: Khadija bint Khuwaylid
desc: Khadija bint Khuwaylid was the first wife of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and a wealthy merchant of the Quraysh of Mecca. She employed Muhammad to manage a trade caravan to Syria and then offered him marriage; sources differ on her age at the time, giving about 28 or 40. Traditional Sunni accounts hold that she was the first person to accept Islam after his first revelation. Sources disagree on how many children they had, most naming six, and Sunni and some Shia views differ on her earlier marriages. She died in November 619, and the year is known as the Year of Sorrow.

name: Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib
desc: Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib was an uncle of the Islamic prophet Muhammad, the father of Ali, and the leader of the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh in Mecca. He took in Muhammad after the death of his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib and, as clan chief, protected him when other Quraysh leaders pressed him to silence his nephew, including during a three-year boycott of the Banu Hashim. He died around 619, within a month of Khadija. His religious status at death is disputed: most Sunni scholars hold that he did not accept Islam, while Shia scholars hold that he was a believer who concealed his faith to protect Muhammad.

name: Battle of Badr
desc: The Battle of Badr was fought on 13 March 624 (17 Ramadan, 2 AH) near Badr, in present-day Saudi Arabia. Muhammad, with an army of about 313 men, defeated a Quraysh force of around 1300 led by Amr ibn Hisham, known to Muslims as Abu Jahl. It began when Muhammad set out to intercept a Meccan caravan under Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, which escaped by another route. About 70 Meccans were killed, including Amr ibn Hisham and Umayya ibn Khalaf, and about 70 were taken prisoner. Muslim tradition calls it a victory owed to divine intervention; other sources credit Muhammad's strategy.

name: Battle of the Trench
desc: The Battle of the Trench was fought in 627, when a confederate force estimated at around 10,000 men, led by the Quraysh with the exiled Banu Nadir and several Bedouin tribes, advanced on Medina. At the suggestion of Salman the Persian, Muhammad's followers dug a trench around the settlement, which held the attackers back for about two weeks until bad weather and quarrels within the confederacy led them to withdraw. Reported casualties were few. The Muslims then besieged the Banu Qurayza, who surrendered, and a judgment pronounced by Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was carried out; scholars doubt Ibn Ishaq's account of the numbers killed.

name: Conquest of Mecca
desc: The conquest of Mecca was a campaign by Muhammad and his companions against the Quraysh-controlled city in December 629 or January 630 (10–20 Ramadan, 8 AH); sources vary on the dates. It followed an attack by the Banu Bakr, with Quraysh support, on the Banu Khuza'ah, allies of the Muslims, which breached the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb sought a renewed truce in Medina without success. Muhammad entered the city, proclaimed a general amnesty with a few exceptions, and cleared the Kaaba of its idols, which tradition numbers at 360. The fall of Mecca formally ended the conflict between the Muslims and the Quraysh.

name: Isra' and Mi'raj
desc: The Isra' and Mi'raj, the Night Travel and Ascension, are Islamic narratives of a night journey in which Muhammad ascends to the heavens, sees the afterlife and returns. The Quran has only brief references, in verses of Surah an-Najm and in the 17th chapter, later called Surah al-Isra'; the detailed accounts come from hadith compiled after his lifetime. In the fuller versions he is accompanied by the angels Gabriel and Michael, meets earlier prophets, and reaches the Sidrat al-Muntaha, where the fifty daily prayers required of him are reduced to five. Classical commentaries mostly read the journey as bodily, Sufism generally as spiritual, and the 27th night of Rajab is widely observed.

name: Farewell Pilgrimage
desc: The Farewell Pilgrimage was the Hajj that Muhammad performed in 10 AH, after the conquest of Mecca. Approximately 100,000 of his companions are said to have gathered to make it with him. He left Medina on 25 Dhu al-Qi'dah, around February 632, and performed Hajj al-Qiran, combining the Umrah and the Hajj. On the 9th of Dhu al-Hijjah, the Day of Arafah, he delivered the Farewell Sermon on Mount Arafat. Muslims believe verse 3 of Surah 5 was revealed after it. His rites on this journey were recorded by those who accompanied him and became a precedent, or sunnah, for later pilgrims.

name: Jabal al-Nour
desc: Jabal al-Nour, the Mountain of the Light, is a mountain of 642 m near Mecca in the Hejaz region of Saudi Arabia. Near its summit is the cave of Hira, where Muhammad is said by Islamic tradition to have received his first revelation, the opening verses of Surah al-Alaq, from the angel Gabriel; the date is traditionally placed on Laylat al-Qadr, around August 610. The cave is about 3.7 m long and lies at 270 m, reached by some 1750 steps. Most Muslims do not count a visit as part of the Hajj, though many climb it, and the mountain is closed to non-Muslims because it lies near Mecca.

name: Ghadir Khumm
desc: Ghadir Khumm was an event of 16 March 632, shortly before Muhammad's death, at a pond near Juhfa between Mecca and Medina, on the return from the Farewell Pilgrimage. Muhammad took Ali by the hand and said, "For whoever I am his mawla, Ali is his mawla." Sunni and Shia Muslims both accept that this was said, but differ on its meaning. Shia Muslims understand mawla as authority and take it as Muhammad's designation of Ali as successor and first Imam, commemorated on 18 Dhu al-Hijjah as Eid al-Ghadir. Sunni Muslims read it as an expression of friendship and esteem rather than a designation of a successor.

name: Imam Ali Shrine
desc: The Imam Ali Shrine is a Shia mosque and mausoleum in Najaf, Iraq, which Shia and Sunni Muslims believe holds the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad. Shias regard Ali as the first Imam and Muhammad's rightful successor; Sunnis count him as the fourth caliph. The Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid built the first structure over the tomb in 786 CE, and later rulers rebuilt and enlarged it, among them the Buyid emir 'Adud al-Dawla, Shah Abbas I and Nader Shah, who gilded the dome in 1742. The present building dates from the Safavid period, with a dome 42 metres high between twin minarets. Millions of pilgrims visit each year.

name: Ahl al-Bayt
desc: Ahl al-Bayt, Arabic for 'People of the House', refers to the family of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Sunni and Shia Muslims both revere it but differ on its religious authority. Shias hold that Muhammad appointed Ali and his descendants, and the largest Shia branch sees the Twelve Imams as divinely guided; Sunnis honour the family without holding the Imams to be divinely appointed or infallible. The term appears in the Quran in verse 33:33, the verse of purification, and Muslims disagree over who belongs to the group. Many traditions name Muhammad, Fatima, Ali, Hasan and Husayn, while some Sunni authors include Muhammad's wives or wider kin such as the Abbasids.

name: Prophet's Mosque
desc: The Prophet's Mosque (al-Masjid al-Nabawi) is a mosque in Medina in the Hejaz, built by Muhammad in 622 after his arrival in the city. Muslim sources say the land belonged to two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, and that Muhammad paid for it with money provided by Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. The first building had a roof of palm trunks, clay and palm leaves, and served as a community centre, court and school. Umar and Uthman enlarged it, and the Umayyad caliph al-Walid I carried out a large expansion in 706 or 707. It now includes the graves of Muhammad, Abu Bakr and Umar beneath the Green Dome, and it is the second holiest site in Islam after Mecca.

name: Hagar
desc: Hagar is an Egyptian woman in the Book of Genesis, the concubine of Abraham and the mother of his firstborn son Ishmael. Genesis says that Sarah, believing herself barren, gave her to Abraham, that tension followed, and that Hagar fled into the desert, where an angel told her to return and promised her many descendants. After Isaac's birth she and Ishmael were sent away and, according to Genesis, God showed her a well. Islamic tradition does not name her in the Quran but describes Hajar as a maid who ran seven times between Safa and Marwah and found the Zamzam well, an act recalled in the Hajj rites. Ishmael is generally taken as the ancestor of the Arabs.

name: Ishmael
desc: Ishmael is the first son of Abraham in the Book of Genesis, born to Hagar, the Egyptian handmaiden of Abraham's wife Sarah. Genesis says he was circumcised at 13, that after Isaac's birth he and Hagar were sent into the wilderness, and that God promised to make of him a great nation; it gives his age at death as 137. Jewish and Islamic traditions regard him as ancestor of the Arabs. Islam honours him as a prophet. Muslim tradition holds that he and Abraham raised the foundations of the Kaaba in Mecca, and that he was buried at the Hijr near it.

name: Isaac
desc: Isaac is the second Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and a figure of the Abrahamic religions. In the Torah he is the son of Abraham and Sarah, father of Jacob and Esau, and grandfather of the twelve tribes of Israel. His name means 'he will laugh', recalling the laughter of his parents when his birth was foretold. Genesis tells of his binding on Mount Moriah, his marriage to Rebekah, and his death at 180. Islam regards him as a prophet and names him seventeen times in the Quran. Some recent scholarship suggests he may originally have been an ancestor revered at a sanctuary in the Beersheba region.

name: Sarah
desc: Sarah, originally Sarai, is the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac in the Book of Genesis, and a matriarch honoured in Judaism, Christianity and Islam. Genesis says she travelled with Abraham to Canaan, gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham when still childless, and, after God renamed her, bore Isaac when Abraham was a hundred. She later asked that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away. According to Genesis she died aged 127 and Abraham bought a cave near Hebron from Ephron the Hittite to bury her, the place later called the Cave of the Patriarchs. Rabbinic tradition links her death to the Binding of Isaac.

name: Binding of Isaac
desc: The Binding of Isaac is the story in Genesis 22 in which, according to the text, God orders Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice on a mountain in the region of Moriah. After Abraham has bound Isaac to an altar, an angel stops him and a ram is sacrificed instead. Jewish tradition interprets it in many ways, among them as a test of Abraham's faith, and some Christian writers saw Isaac as foreshadowing Christ. In the Quran the son is unnamed; early scholars disagreed whether he was Isaac or Ishmael, and Muslims commemorate the submission of Abraham and his son at Eid al-Adha. Some scholars suggest an older version in which Isaac was killed.

name: Cave of the Patriarchs
desc: The Cave of the Patriarchs, called Machpelah in Hebrew and the Ibrahimi Mosque by Muslims, is a series of caves in the Old City of Hebron in the West Bank. According to Genesis, Abraham bought the cave and its field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place for Sarah; Judaism, Christianity and Islam hold it holy as the tomb of the patriarchs and their wives. A large enclosure built under Herod the Great stands over it. A Byzantine basilica was later built there, and after the Muslim conquest the building became a mosque. Since the Six-Day War of 1967 it has been divided between a mosque and a synagogue. In February 1994 Baruch Goldstein killed 29 Palestinian Muslims there.

name: Four Noble Truths
desc: The Four Noble Truths are a central teaching of Buddhism: dukkha, usually rendered suffering or unsatisfactoriness; its origin in craving and attachment; its cessation, or nirvana; and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to that cessation. Buddhist tradition identifies them as the Buddha's first teaching, set out in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Some scholars hold that this identification was made later and that the formulation developed over time. Theravada tradition gave them great importance by about the 5th century CE, while Mahayana places more weight on emptiness and the bodhisattva path. Western presentations since the 19th century often present them as its central teaching.

name: Noble Eightfold Path
desc: The Noble Eightfold Path is an early summary of Buddhist practice leading to liberation from samsara, the cycle of rebirth, in nirvana. Its eight parts are right view, right resolve, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right samadhi. It is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths. Theravada tradition also groups it as morality, meditation and insight. The Indologist Tilmann Vetter suggests that the early description of the path may have been as simple as the Middle Way, later elaborated into eight factors. In Buddhist symbolism the path is often shown as the eight spokes of the dharma wheel.

name: Bodhi tree
desc: The Bodhi tree is the sacred fig (Ficus religiosa) at the Mahabodhi Temple in Bodh Gaya, Bihar, India, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha Gautama attained enlightenment beneath a Bo tree at this site and became the Buddha, around the 5th century BCE. The original tree no longer survives. Recorded episodes of destruction include its felling in the reign of Aśoka (c. 268–232 BCE) and its cutting down by King Śaśāṅka of Gauda around 600 CE, and each time it was replanted from saplings. A sapling taken to Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka survives as the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, and the present tree at Bodh Gaya was planted in 1881 from a cutting of it.

name: Maya (mother of the Buddha)
desc: Maya, also called Mahāmāyā and Māyādevī, was Queen of the Shakya and the mother of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha. She was the wife of King Śuddhodana. Buddhist tradition holds that she dreamed of a white elephant entering her side before the birth, and that her son was born in the gardens of Lumbini while she was travelling to her family home in Devadaha. The commentaries say she died about seven days later and was reborn in a Buddhist heaven, as is said to happen to the mothers of all Buddhas. Her sister Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī raised the child. In Buddhist art she is most often shown giving birth while holding the branch of a tree.

name: Yaśodharā
desc: Yaśodharā, originally called Bhaddakaccānā in Pāli, was the wife of Prince Siddhartha before he renounced the household life, and the mother of Rāhula. Buddhist texts describe her as a Koliya princess, daughter of Suppabuddha, who married Siddhartha when both were 16. Tradition holds that he left the palace on the night their son was born, when she was 29. Texts say she lived simply during his six-year absence and later asked Rāhula to go to the Buddha to ask for his inheritance. She was ordained as a bhikkhunī among the five hundred women who followed Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, is considered an arahat, and is said to have died at 78, two years before the Buddha.

name: Rāhula
desc: Rāhula was the son of Prince Siddhārtha, later the Buddha, and of Yaśodharā. The Pāli tradition says he was born on the day of his father's renunciation, when the prince was 29, and was named for a "fetter" on the path; the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition says he was conceived that day and born six years later. When the Buddha returned to his hometown, Yaśodharā had Rāhula ask for the throne of the Śākya clan, and the Buddha instead had him ordained as the first Buddhist novice monk. Early accounts state that Rāhula died before the Buddha, while later tradition holds that he outlived him. The earliest texts give little detail about him.

name: Ānanda
desc: Ānanda was the primary attendant of the Buddha and one of his ten principal disciples, remembered for his memory. In early Buddhist texts he was the Buddha's first cousin, and he became attendant twenty years into the Buddha's ministry, accompanying him for the rest of his life. He requested on behalf of Mahāpajāpati Gotamī that women be allowed to be ordained, and he was with the Buddha in his last year. Tradition holds that he became enlightened just before the First Council, where he recited the Buddha's discourses and was also reproved by Mahākassapa. Scholars are skeptical about the historicity of many events of his life. He is said to have died 20 years after the Buddha.

name: Devadatta
desc: Devadatta was, by tradition, a Buddhist monk, cousin and brother-in-law of Gautama Siddhārtha. Accounts of his life vary greatly. The Theravāda Vinaya says he sought to lead the Sangha, won the support of Prince Ajātashatru and tried to kill the Buddha, and it names five austerities he urged on monks, which the Buddha would not make obligatory. Pilgrims such as Faxian recorded followers of Devadatta centuries later. Scholars differ on how to read the stories: Reginald Ray regards them as a later Sthavira legend, while Bhikkhu Sujato argues the core episodes go back to the time of the Buddha. The Lotus Sūtra says that he too will become a Buddha.

name: Buddhist councils
desc: Buddhist councils were gatherings of the monastic community, the sangha, held to recite and correct the teachings and settle disputes of discipline. The term saṅgīti means "reciting together". Tradition places the First Council at Rājagṛha soon after the Buddha's death, where Ānanda is said to have recited the discourses and Upāli the Vinaya. The Second Council is said to have met at Vaiśālī a century later over lax practices. Theravāda sources add a Third Council under Ashoka at Pāṭaliputra and a Sri Lankan council in the 1st century BCE that wrote down the canon. Modern scholars question the historicity of several of these councils, and a Fifth Council met at Mandalay in 1871.

name: Middle Way
desc: The Middle Way, or Middle Path, is a Buddhist term for two aspects of the Buddha's teaching. The first is a spiritual practice that avoids both extreme asceticism and sensual indulgence, and is defined as the Noble Eightfold Path leading to awakening. The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, which Buddhist tradition regards as the Buddha's first teaching after his awakening, presents it this way, addressing five ascetics. The second is teaching the Dharma "by the middle", which avoids both eternalism and annihilationism in speaking of existence and personal identity. Y. Karunadasa notes it is not a compromise between the extremes.

name: Parinirvana
desc: In Buddhism, parinirvana is the state entered at death by someone who attained nirvana during life. It means release from samsara, karma and rebirth, and the ending of the aggregates (skandhas) that make up a being. Modern usage tends to keep "nirvana" for the awakening experience and "parinirvana" for the death. Accounts of the Buddha's parinirvana at Kuśinagara are found in the Pāli Mahāparinibbāna Sutta and its Sanskrit and Chinese parallels. Bareau judged only the death and funeral rites to be the oldest core. Some Mahāyāna scriptures, notably the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, describe it as the realm of the eternal true Self of the Tathāgata.

name: Tirthankara
desc: In Jainism, a Tirthaṅkara, literally a "ford-maker", is a supreme preacher of the dharma who establishes a passage across saṃsāra, the cycle of birth and death. Jains hold that after attaining kevala jñāna, or omniscience, a Tirthaṅkara teaches and organises a fourfold sangha of monks, nuns and male and female lay followers. Jain cosmology says that 24 appear in each half of the time cycle, with Rishabhanatha first in the present one and Mahavira, traditionally dated 599–527 BCE, the 24th. Academic consensus broadly accepts Parshvanatha, the 23rd, and Mahavira as historical figures. Their teachings form the basis of the Jain canons.

name: Kalpa Sūtra
desc: The Kalpa Sūtra is a Jain scripture containing the biographies of the Tirthankaras, notably Parshvanatha and Mahavira. It is ascribed to Acharya Bhadrabahu, which would place it in the 4th century BCE, and it states that it was written down 980 or 993 years after Mahavira's nirvana. From the mid-15th century it was frequently illustrated with miniature paintings, and the oldest surviving copies are on paper from western India in the 14th century. It is read during the eight-day festival of Paryushan, and Jain tradition regards the sound of its words as transforming the listener's soul.

name: Anekantavada
desc: Anekantavada, from the Sanskrit for "many-sidedness", is the Jain doctrine that ultimate truth and reality are complex and have multiple aspects and viewpoints. Jainism holds that no single statement can describe existence, and that complete knowledge (Kevala Jnana) is comprehended only by the Arihants. Jain tradition traces it to the teachings of Mahavira and his predecessors, while its details emerged in the 1st millennium CE from debates among Jain, Buddhist and Vedic scholars. Syadvada and nayavada later gave it logical structure. Jain texts illustrate it with the parable of the blind men and an elephant.

name: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur
desc: Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur is a gurdwara in Kartarpur, in the Narowal District of Punjab, Pakistan, beside the Ravi River. It stands on the site where, in Sikh tradition, Guru Nanak settled and gathered the Sikh community after his journeys, living there for 18 years until his death in 1539. The main shrine was built in 1925 with funds from the Maharaja of Patiala, repaired in 1995 and fully restored in 2004. A new courtyard, museum and library were added in November 2018. The shrine lies near the India-Pakistan border, and the Kartarpur Corridor, opened on 9 November 2019, gave Indian pilgrims visa-free access.

name: Bhai Mardana
desc: Bhai Mardana was a musician born to a Mirasi Muslim family of Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, and a lifelong companion of Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism. He played the rabab while Nanak sang his hymns, and became one of Nanak's first disciples. The Miharban Janam Sakhi says he was ten years older than Nanak and his companion from childhood. The janamsakhis portray him as the doubting traveller whose questions draw out the Guru's message. The Puratan Janam Sakhi relates that, when he fell ill at Kartarpur, Nanak told him his body could be disposed of as he pleased. Three of Nanak's shlokas addressed to him are in the Guru Granth Sahib.

name: Guru Angad
desc: Guru Angad was the second of the ten Sikh gurus. Born Lehna, a Khatri and a worshipper of the goddess Durga, he met Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, served him there, and was named Angad, "my own limb", as successor in 1539. After Nanak's death on 22 September 1539 he led the community from Khadur Sahib, though few Sikhs at first accepted him because Nanak's sons also claimed the succession. He is remembered for formalising the Gurmukhi alphabet, although scholars note the script pre-dates Sikhism, and for systematising langar. He contributed 62 or 63 saloks and chose Amar Das, not his own son, as successor. He died on 29 March 1552.

name: Nankana Sahib
desc: Nankana Sahib is a city in central Punjab, Pakistan, about 91 km west of Lahore and the headquarters of its district. It is named for Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, who was born and based there, and its birthplace gurdwara is among the holiest Sikh sites. A town called Rai-Bhoi-Di-Talwandi was founded there under the Delhi Sultanate by Rai Bhoi, and his great-grandson Rai Bular Bhatti renamed it after the birth of Guru Nanak. Maharaja Ranjit Singh renovated the main gurdwara in 1819–20. On 20 February 1921 the Udasi mahant ordered his men to fire on Akali protesters, an event called the Nankana massacre. The city had 130,041 people in 2023.

name: Mul Mantar
desc: The Mul Mantar is the opening verse of the Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, a twelve-word statement in Punjabi in the Gurmukhi script. It is the best known of Sikh texts and summarises the teaching of Guru Nanak. After Ik Onkar, its words literally mean true name, the creator, without fear, without hate, timeless in form, beyond birth, self-existent, known by the grace of the Guru. Translators differ over the first two words, rendering them "There is one god" or "One reality is". The verse is repeated before many hymns. It existed in several versions in the 16th century, and Guru Arjan gave it its final form in the 17th.

name: Langar
desc: In Sikhism, a langar is the community kitchen of a gurdwara, serving free meals to all regardless of religion, caste, gender, economic status or ethnicity. Visitors sit on the floor and eat together, volunteers work as seva, and the food is always lacto-vegetarian. Sikh tradition credits Guru Nanak with introducing it around 1500 CE as a symbol of equality, though free kitchens existed earlier in the region, including among Sufi missionaries. Guru Angad is remembered for systematising the langar in all gurdwaras. Guru Amar Das made it prominent by requiring that people dine together regardless of caste and class.

name: Aaron
desc: According to the Hebrew Bible, Aaron was an Israelite prophet, high priest and elder brother of Moses; information about him comes only from religious texts. Exodus relates that he served as Moses' spokesman before Pharaoh. Part of the Law given at Sinai granted the priesthood to him and his male descendants, and the kohanim are traditionally held to descend from him. The Bible tells how he made the golden calf, while the Quran attributes it to Samiri. Numbers says he died aged 123 on Mount Hor, whereas Deuteronomy places his death at Moseroth. Many historians think Aaronide families did not control the priesthood before the Babylonian exile.

name: Miriam
desc: Miriam is described in the Hebrew Bible as the daughter of Amram and Jochebed and the older sister of Moses and Aaron. The Torah calls her a prophetess, and the Talmud names her among the seven major female prophets of Israel. Tradition identifies her with the unnamed sister who watched the infant Moses on the Nile. In Exodus she leads the Israelites in the Song of the Sea. In Numbers she and Aaron speak against Moses over his "Cushite" wife, and she is afflicted with a skin disease and shut out of the camp for seven days. The Torah records that she died and was buried at Kadesh. The Quran also has her follow the infant Moses.

name: Burning bush
desc: The burning bush is an event recorded in the Book of Exodus and in Islamic scripture, in which a bush burns on Mount Horeb without being consumed. In the biblical account an angel of the Lord appears in a flame from the bush, and God calls to Moses, who was grazing Jethro's flocks, telling him to take off his sandals because the place is sacred. The voice names itself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and sends Moses to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. It gives its name as Yahweh, linked to the phrase "I Am Who I Am". Some Old Testament scholars see the account as joined from Yahwist and Elohist texts.

name: Plagues of Egypt
desc: In the Book of Exodus, the Plagues of Egypt are ten disasters that Yahweh inflicts on the Egyptians to persuade Pharaoh to free the enslaved Israelites. They run from the Nile turned to blood, frogs, gnats and flies through the death of livestock, boils, hail, locusts and three days of darkness, to the death of the firstborn. Jews recite the plagues during the Passover Seder. Modern scholars broadly hold that the Exodus is not a historical account of the origins of the Israelites. Biblical scholars have dismissed natural explanations, such as a volcanic eruption for the darkness, because the plagues' pattern, timing and control by Moses mark them as supernatural in the text.

name: Parting of the Red Sea
desc: The Parting of the Red Sea is an episode of the Exodus in the Hebrew Bible. According to the Book of Exodus, the Israelites led by Moses were pursued by the Egyptian army; at God's command Moses held out his staff, the waters of the Yam Suph parted, and the Israelites crossed on dry ground. When the Egyptians followed, the waters returned and drowned them. The Quran also relates the crossing, and Muslims fast two days in Muharram to commemorate it. No archaeological evidence directly supports the account apart from the biblical text, and scholars debate where the crossing took place, since Yam Suph is literally a sea or lake of reeds.

name: Golden calf
desc: The golden calf is a cult image that, according to the Book of Exodus, the Israelites made while Moses was on Mount Sinai. The narrative says Aaron collected gold earrings and ornaments and fashioned the calf; Moses, on seeing it, broke the tablets, burned the calf, and the Levites killed some three thousand people. The Quran also tells of a calf made in his absence. Scholars note that bull imagery was widespread in the ancient Near East and compare Exodus 32 with the golden calves of 1 Kings 12. The apostle Paul cites the episode in 1 Corinthians as a warning against idolatry.

name: Mount Nebo
desc: Mount Nebo is a ridge in Jordan, about 700 metres above sea level, part of the Abarim range. According to Deuteronomy, Moses climbed it in the land of Moab, saw the Promised Land that he was not to enter, and died there; the text says his burial place was unknown. On the summit, called Syagha, excavators found a Byzantine church and monastery, first built in the second half of the 4th century to commemorate Moses' death. A pilgrim named Aetheria mentions the church in 394. Pope John Paul II and Pope Benedict XVI have visited the site.

name: Tabernacle
desc: According to the Hebrew Bible, the Tabernacle was the portable dwelling of Yahweh used by the Israelites from the Exodus until the conquest of Canaan. Exodus 25–31 and 35–40 describe it: a Holy of Holies containing the Ark of the Covenant, behind a veil, and an outer sanctuary with a lamp-stand, a table for showbread and an altar of incense. Those who read the books of Kings literally hold that Solomon's Temple replaced it after 480 years in the Masoretic Text or 440 in the Septuagint. Scholars compare it with tent shrines of Canaan, Babylonia and Egypt, among them a Midianite tent shrine at Timna.

name: Joshua
desc: Joshua, whose Hebrew name Yehoshua means 'Yahweh is salvation', was Moses' assistant in Exodus and Numbers and, in the Book of Joshua, his successor as leader of the Israelite tribes. The Bible names him as one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan, and says he led the conquest of the land, including the fall of Jericho, and allocated it to the tribes. It gives his age at death as 110. Muslims honour him as Yusha bin Nun, understood to be Moses' attendant in the Quran. Mainstream scholarship holds that the Book of Joshua is a theological narrative compiled centuries after the supposed conquest, and that archaeology largely contradicts its account.

name: Midian
desc: Midian was a region in the Tabuk Province of modern Saudi Arabia, on the east shore of the Gulf of Aqaba, mentioned in the Hebrew Bible and the Quran. The Bible makes Midian a son of Abraham and Keturah and says Moses spent forty years there, marrying Zipporah, daughter of the priest Jethro. Some scholars think the name first denoted a tribal confederation. Midianite pottery, also called Qurayyah Painted Ware, is found from the southern Levant to north-west Arabia, and a Midianite tent shrine at the copper-mining site of Timna offers a close parallel to the biblical Tabernacle.

name: Zipporah
desc: Zipporah appears in the Book of Exodus as the wife of Moses and a daughter of Jethro, the priest of Midian. According to Exodus, Moses defended Jethro's daughters at a well in Midian, and Jethro gave her to him. She bore two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. In an obscure passage at an inn on the road to Egypt, she circumcises her son and God spares Moses; the details are debated. Later, Jethro brings her and her sons to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. Numbers 12 mentions a Cushite wife of Moses, and interpreters differ on whether this is Zipporah.

name: Gathas
desc: The Gathas are the central texts of Zoroastrianism, composed in Old or Gathic Avestan and often attributed to Zarathustra himself. They comprise five poems of seventeen hymns, with 238 stanzas and 897 verses, and survive within the Yasna liturgy. They are the oldest attestation of an Iranian language. Scholars are divided on whether Zarathustra wrote them. Zoroastrian tradition places him in the 6th century BCE, but many scholars now accept a date near 1000 BCE, some as early as 1500 BCE. The texts describe a simple society of nomadic pastoralists.

name: Vishtaspa
desc: Vishtaspa is a figure in Zoroastrian scripture and tradition, portrayed as an early follower and patron of Zoroaster who helped spread his message. The Gathas speak of him as Zoroaster's ally, and later Avestan hymns describe his struggles against enemies of the faith. Zoroastrian tradition presents him as a righteous king ruling from Bactria. In the Sistan cycle texts, by contrast, he is a loathsome ruler of the Kayanian dynasty, and Greco-Roman writers knew prophecies written under his name. He is not attested in inscriptions, and is traditionally assumed to be historical, though obscured by later accretions.

name: Amesha Spenta
desc: In Zoroastrianism, the Amesha Spenta, literally 'Immortal (which is) holy', are seven divine entities emanating from Ahura Mazda, through whom, in tradition, all later creation was accomplished. The doctrine is only alluded to in the Avesta and is set out in later Middle Persian texts such as the Bundahishn. In the Gathas each represents a moral quality, such as truth or good thought, that people should strive to acquire, and each has an opposing counterpart. Each is linked to one of the seven creations. The first seven days of the Zoroastrian month are dedicated to them.

name: Yasna
desc: Yasna is the Avestan name both of a text of the Avesta and of the Yasna liturgy, Zoroastrianism's principal act of worship. The ceremony is meant to strengthen the ordered creation of Ahura Mazda against the destructive forces of Angra Mainyu, and culminates in the offering to the waters. A trained priest recites it in about two hours, in the morning. The text has 72 chapters composed at different times, including the oldest of the canon: the four most sacred prayers and the five Gathas, which tradition holds were composed by Zoroaster himself.

name: Ahriman
desc: Ahriman, in Avestan Angra Mainyu, is the destructive evil spirit of Zoroastrianism, the main adversary either of the Spenta Mainyu or directly of Ahura Mazda. In the Gathas, the oldest texts, angra mainyu is not yet a proper name but describes a destructive spirit set against the bounteous one. In the Younger Avesta and the Pahlavi texts, including the Bundahishn completed in the 12th century, he opposes Ahura Mazda's creation with his own, and Zoroastrian tradition holds that he will be defeated. Zurvanite sources make him the twin brother of Ohrmuzd. In 1862 Martin Haug proposed that he was a creature of Ahura Mazda, a view widely held by Zoroastrians today.

name: Wu wei
desc: Wu wei (無為) is a concept of ancient Chinese philosophy that literally means not-acting or non-doing, and is variously translated as actionlessness, inaction or effortless action. In Daoism it describes the way the Tao acts, silently and without force, and Daoists aspire to live in alignment with it. The idea appears as early as the Spring and Autumn period and also figures in the Confucian Analects and in Legalist statecraft, where it names a ruler who leaves details to his ministers. Scholars such as Herrlee G. Creel distinguished the Zhuangzi's wu wei, a detachment from human affairs, from that of the Tao Te Ching, a technique for governing.

name: Tao
desc: The Tao or Dao (道) is, in East Asian philosophy and religions, the source and fundamental principle of the universe. The Chinese character means way, path or road, and philosophically doctrine or principle. According to the Tao Te Ching, Tao is self-existent, formless, eternal and the source of all existence, and it is said to be beyond description; the text distinguishes the named Tao from the unnamed Tao. It describes Tao as feminine, a mother of all things, and Taoist scriptures treat the Ultra Supreme Elder Lord as an embodiment of it. Scholars distinguish its ethical use in Confucianism and religious Taoism from its more metaphysical use in philosophical Taoism.

name: Yinxi
desc: Yinxi is a figure of Zhou China known from later accounts, said to have been a guard at the western gate of the Zhou capital Chengzhou, present-day Luoyang, or alternatively at the western pass out of the Luo–Yi valley. He is said to have recognised the wisdom of Laozi, halted him on his way through the gate and persuaded him to compose the Tao Te Ching before letting him pass. He is later credited with a book called Guan Yi, revered by later scholars, and came to be regarded as a sage. His own work, the Perfect Classic of the Beginning of the Scripture of the Supreme Way, was lost in the Han period, and later versions were considered forgeries.
